title: The three gates
hookLine: the Gita's 'demonic' is a way of living, entered by desire, anger and greed
carry: desire, anger and greed, the three gates of hell

cards: Hear the word demonic and you probably picture horns, fire, a horror movie. The Gita's picture is quieter, and more unsettling. It's a person lying awake at night, running the numbers.
I got this today. Tomorrow I'll get that. This is mine, and that will be mine too.
I beat that rival, and I'll beat the others. Who is like me? It sounds less like a monster and more like a very busy, very anxious person.
Maybe someone most of us have been, for an evening or two.

teach.b: Verse six: there are two kinds of beings in this world, the divine and the asuric, usually translated demonic.

In Hindu stories the asuras are the gods' rivals, powerful and proud, like Mahishasura, the buffalo demon who seized heaven and still wanted more, until the Goddess Durga brought him down, the victory many Hindus celebrate at Navratri.

Here the word describes a way of living. Verses seven and eight: such people don't know when to act and when to hold back. They say the world has no truth, no ground, no God, and runs on desire alone.

Verse ten: gripped by desire that can never be filled, full of hypocrisy, pride and arrogance. Then verses twelve to fifteen, the monologue from the hook. Bound by hundreds of hopes, they pile up wealth by any means.

teach.h: THIS IS MINE. WHO IS LIKE ME?
teach.b: This I gained today, this wish I'll fulfill. I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am successful, strong and happy. Who else is like me?
Even their rituals, verse seventeen says, are done for show. The Gita's verdict is severe: this road leads downward, again and again.
Many teachers, especially modern ones, read this chapter less as a label for other people and more as a mirror, though some classical commentators read it as a portrait of a kind of soul.
Then verse twenty-one names where it all starts: three gates to hell that destroy the self.
Kama, desire; krodha, anger; and lobha, greed.
Shut those three, the Gita says, and a person begins to walk toward the highest. That's the teaching: the gates aren't groups of people. They're three movements inside anyone.

how: At Navratri and Durga Puja many Hindus remember Durga's victory over the asura Mahishasura; teachers often read Gita 16 as a mirror for self-examination rather than a way to label others, and the three gates of 16.21, kama, krodha and lobha, are widely quoted.

o: a curse laid on a family line by an enemy
a proud, grasping way of living, not a monster
evil spirits that possess people from outside

games.q: the other inheritance — tap the pairs.
p: the gods' proud rivals in the stories

s: the Gita's 'demonic' person is pictured with horns and fire
it's a person running a monologue: this is mine, who is like me?
the three gates in 16.21 are desire, anger and greed
kama, krodha, lobha: three movements inside anyone.

games.q: the Gita names three gates that lead a person down. what are they?
games.why: desire, anger and greed, 16.21. the gates are movements inside a person, not outside threats.

practice: Listen for the monologue: something to get, someone to beat, something that's mine. Don't argue with it; just hear it, the way you'd hear a radio in another room.
Then check the three gates, desire pulling, anger simmering, a grasping for more, and wherever one is open, breathe out slowly and let it close a little.

wordCard.voice: The demonic. Gita sixteen: the asuric way of living, restless, proud and grasping, and the three gates that lead there: desire, anger and greed.

orig.note: Sanskrit: asura, in the stories the proud rivals of the devas; Gita 16 uses 'asuri', asuric, for a way of living.

carryVoice: Your line: desire, anger and greed, the three gates of hell. Shut them, the Gita says, and you start toward the highest. Two hundred fourteen days in.
